title: Agent safety: deterministic guardrails and verifiers
seriesDescription: Topic-by-topic JEE-style quizzes for the backend and AI-engineering interview roadmap: integer, assertion-reason, matrix match, fill-in-the-blanks, short code writing, plus multi-correct questions. Language core, concurrency, DSA, web frameworks, data access, databases, messaging, resilience, security, testing, system design, LLM and agent engineering.
description: Why safety belongs in code rather than prompts: schema validation, allow-lists, a sqlglot SELECT-only guard, read-only roles, verifiers and defence in depth for LLM agents.
source: sqlglot docs; Pydantic v2 docs; OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications; Anthropic and OpenAI agent-safety guidance; Simon Willison on prompt injection

questions.prompt: Using sqlglot, write is_select_only(sql) -> bool for LLM-generated PostgreSQL. Return True only if the text parses into exactly one statement whose root node is a SELECT (exp.Select). Return False on a parse error.
questions.explanation: Other solutions pass (parse_one plus a check that no extra statement exists, or walking the tree for Insert/Delete/Drop nodes). Real systems add more: UNION and INTERSECT parse as set operations, and in PostgreSQL SELECT ... INTO can create a table, so also use a read-only database role, a statement timeout and a LIMIT.

questions.prompt: A guard accepts SQL only if it parses into exactly one statement whose root node is a plain SELECT. Of these five inputs, how many pass: (1) SELECT 1; (2) SELECT 1; DROP TABLE t; (3) WITH x AS (SELECT 1) SELECT * FROM x; (4) SELECT 1 UNION SELECT 2; (5) DELETE FROM t?
questions.explanation: Inputs 1 and 3 pass (a WITH clause hangs off the SELECT node). Input 2 has two statements, input 4 has a Union root rather than a Select, and input 5 is a Delete. Union is a common false rejection, so a production guard usually allows set operations explicitly.

questions.prompt: Write a Pydantic v2 model RefundArgs for an LLM tool call: order_id is a string that must match ORD- followed by exactly six digits, and amount is a float greater than 0 and at most 500.

checks.label: pattern mentions ORD- and six digits

questions.explanation: In Pydantic v1 the argument was regex=. A field_validator or Annotated constraints also pass. Validate model output against this before the tool runs; reject, do not coerce silently.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion (A) and the reason (R), then choose the correct option.
questions.assertion: Safety rules such as "never delete data" should be enforced in code, not only stated in the prompt.
questions.reason: A prompt is a request to the model, not an enforcement mechanism, whereas code checks run the same way every time.

whys.a: Correct: the model may ignore, misread or be tricked out of an instruction, while a code check cannot be argued with.
whys.b: R is the direct reason, so it explains A.

questions.explanation: Use the prompt for behaviour and tone; use code for anything with a cost if violated.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion (A) and the reason (R), then choose the correct option.
questions.assertion: For which tools an agent may call, an allow-list is safer than a deny-list.
questions.reason: Python sets give constant-time membership tests.

whys.a: R is true but speed is not why allow-lists are safer.
whys.b: Correct: unknown tools are rejected by default (A), and O(1) lookup (R) is true but irrelevant to safety.
whys.d: A is true: deny-lists miss new or renamed items.

questions.explanation: Default deny: anything not named is refused.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion (A) and the reason (R), then choose the correct option.
questions.assertion: Running LLM-generated SQL under a read-only database role adds defence in depth even when a parser guard exists.
questions.reason: Once the application validates the SQL, the database role no longer matters.

whys.a: R is false, so it cannot explain A.
whys.b: R is false, not just unrelated.
whys.c: Correct: A is true because parsers have gaps and bugs, so layers matter. R is false: it is the very argument defence in depth rejects.

questions.explanation: Pair the role with a statement timeout, row limit and least-privilege views that hide sensitive columns.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion (A) and the reason (R), then choose the correct option.
questions.assertion: Blocking the keyword DROP with a regular expression is a robust SQL safety guard.
questions.reason: SQL can be varied with case, comments, quoting and other statements, so keyword filters are easy to bypass.

whys.b: A is false, so the pair is not both-true.
whys.c: R is true, so this option is wrong.
whys.d: Correct: A is false, R is true. Parse the SQL into an AST and allow-list node types instead.

questions.explanation: Also note that DROP is not the only danger: DELETE, UPDATE, COPY, pg_sleep and file functions matter too.

questions.prompt: Match each control to the risk it mitigates.

right.text: The model calls a tool it should not have
Leaking emails or phone numbers to the user
Result sets that exhaust memory or context

questions.explanation: Interviewers like a table of control versus threat, plus the point that no single control is enough.

questions.text: Guardrails that run in {1} are deterministic and testable, a prompt instruction is only {2}, and for tools you prefer an {3} over a deny-list.
questions.explanation: Deterministic checks can be unit-tested, replayed from logs and audited; prompts cannot.

questions.prompt: An agent issues refunds and the rule is "never refund more than the order total". Which is the strongest control?

options.text: Code compares amount with the stored order total first.
options.why: Right: the rule is enforced in code against the source of truth.

options.text: Add "never refund more than the order total" in capital letters to the system prompt.
options.why: The model can still be talked out of it or err.

options.text: Ask a second model whether the refund looks reasonable before proceeding with the payment.
options.why: A model judge is probabilistic and can be persuaded too.

options.text: Trust the amount supplied by the customer in the chat when it seems plausible to the agent.

questions.explanation: Verify against authoritative data, not against what the model or user claims.

questions.prompt: Which properties of an agent answer can a deterministic verifier check? Select all that apply.

options.text: The output parses as JSON that matches the required schema.
Every cited document id exists in the set of retrieved documents.
The invoice line items add up to the stated total.
The reply sounds friendly and empathetic to the customer.
options.why: Tone is subjective and needs a model or human judge.

questions.explanation: Use deterministic checks wherever possible, then LLM judges for the subjective remainder.

questions.prompt: A policy says refunds strictly above $100 need approval. An agent plans 40 refunds: 20 of $50, 12 of $100 and 8 of $250. How many need approval?
questions.explanation: Only the eight $250 refunds exceed $100. The twelve $100 refunds equal the limit, so they do not need approval under "strictly above". Boundary conditions like this are classic guard bugs.

questions.prompt: True or false: asking a second LLM to check the first LLM's output is a deterministic guardrail.

options.why: Correct: a second model is still probabilistic and can be manipulated; it is a useful extra layer but not a replacement for code checks.

questions.explanation: Layer them: code checks first, model judges second, human review for high risk.
